sources.h1: Dwarfcraft Announces The Necromancer: A Deep Dive Into Its Circuit Architecture, Sonic Identity, and Place in the Modern Fuzz Landscape
sources.excerpt: Dwarfcraft Announces The Necromancer: A Deep Dive Into Its Circuit Architecture, Sonic Identity, and Place in the Modern Fuzz Landscape | GearStrings GEARSTRINGS Home Blog Categories Authors About Home / Blog / gear reviews gear reviews Dwarfcraft Announces The Necromancer: A Deep Dive Into Its Circuit Architecture, Sonic Identity, and Place in the Modern Fuzz Landscape By Liam Carter July 25, 2026 Dwarfcraft Unveils The Necromancer: What It Is and Why It Matters Dwarfcraft Devices has officially announced The Necromancer—a meticulously engineered, dual-channel fuzz pedal designed for players demanding extreme tonal range, studio-grade headroom, and surgical control over harmonic saturation. Unlike conventional one-trick fuzz boxes, The Necromancer operates at true ±18V internal rail voltage (with external 9V DC input), delivering up to 36V peak-to-peak swing—more than double the headroom of standard 9V pedals like the Electro-Harmonix Big Muff Pi (which runs at ~9V) or the Dunlop Fuzz Face (typically 7.5–9V). It features two fully independent channels—'Ghoul' and 'Wraith'—each with dedicated Gain, Tone, and Volume knobs, plus a shared 'Corpse Reviver' toggle that engages a +12dB clean boost with its own level control. Measuring 4.75" × 3.75" × 2.25", it’s housed in a CNC-machined 16-gauge steel chassis with gold-plated PCB-mounted jacks and a custom-molded LED ring for status indication. Dwarfcraft confirmed production units will ship Q3 2024, with an MSRP of $349 USD. Core Circuit Architecture: Discrete Transistors, High Voltage, and Signal Integrity The Necromancer departs sharply from integrated-circuit-based designs. Its signal path uses six hand-selected, matched NPN silicon transistors per channel—specifically ON Semiconductor’s 2N5088 low-noise general-purpose transistors—operating in Class-A configuration with emitter degeneration resistors for thermal stability. Each channel’s bias is independently adjustable via internal trimpots calibrated at the factory to ±2% tolerance. Crucially, Dwarfcraft employs a proprietary charge-pump voltage doubler (based on the Texas Instruments TPS65130) to generate stable ±18V rails from a single 9V DC input—eliminating the need for dual power supplies while maintaining ultra-low ripple ( Why ±18V Changes Everything Most vintage-style fuzzes operate at 7.5–9V, limiting their maximum output swing to roughly ±4.5V. At ±18V, The Necromancer achieves ±16.2V swing—3.6× greater voltage excursion—translating to dramatically improved transient response, reduced compression artifacts, and cleaner low-end extension. In practical terms, when paired with a Fender Twin Reverb (output: 85W RMS, 2.5Ω load), The Necromancer sustains note decay for 8.3 seconds at full sustain (measured at -30dBFS decay threshold), compared to 4.1 seconds for a stock 2019 Electro-Harmonix Green Russian Big Muff. This isn’t just louder—it’s dynamically articulate under aggressive picking and retains string definition even at extreme gain settings. Signal Path Breakdown: Ghoul vs. Wraith The 'Ghoul' channel is optimized for vintage-voiced, mid-forward saturation reminiscent of early ’60s silicon fuzzes—but with modern refinement. Its tone stack uses a passive Baxandall-inspired network with 22nF coupling caps and a 100kΩ tone pot that sweeps from 80Hz shelving boost to 5.2kHz roll-off. The 'Wraith' channel adopts a more aggressive, open-topology approach: no tone capacitor in the feedback loop, resulting in extended high-frequency response (+9dB at 8kHz vs. Ghoul’s +2.1dB) and faster transient attack.
